Pregnancy

High triglycerides in pregnancy: results, risks and treatment

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Triglycerides normally rise during pregnancy, especially later on. A raised result therefore needs interpretation alongside the stage of pregnancy, previous results and other health conditions. Very high levels need a clear clinical plan because they can inflame the pancreas. Food changes can help, but a severe result should not be managed with a restrictive diet or fish-oil capsules on your own.

What triglycerides do, and why pregnancy changes them

Triglycerides are fats made from a glycerol backbone and three fatty acids. They circulate in blood and provide stored energy. They come from food and are also made by the liver; they are different from cholesterol, although both appear on a lipid blood test.

Pregnancy changes hormones, insulin sensitivity and the way fat is stored and released. Levels often rise as pregnancy progresses and can be two to three times their earlier level. This helps support changing energy needs, but a physiological rise does not make every high result harmless. A non-pregnant reference value below 150 mg/dL is not a universal upper limit for every stage of pregnancy.

Read the number in context

Ask which units the laboratory uses, whether the sample was fasting and how the result compares with your earlier tests. Fasting triglycerides of 500 mg/dL or more, approximately 5.6–5.7 mmol/L, are considered severe. Pancreatitis risk increases at this level and rises particularly at 1,000 mg/dL, approximately 11.3 mmol/L, or more. These are management thresholds, not proof that pancreatitis has occurred or that a lower result carries no risk.

Contact the team managing your pregnancy promptly about a severe result rather than waiting for symptoms or the next routine appointment. A result around 1,000 mg/dL or higher needs an urgent specialist management plan even if you feel well. The team decides repeat fasting tests and monitoring frequency; higher-risk pregnancies may need testing more often as the third trimester progresses.

Look for inherited and treatable contributors

A family tendency to high triglycerides can become more apparent during pregnancy. Previous very high results, pancreatitis or a close relative with these problems are useful information. High triglycerides are not simply evidence of eating badly or a reason to blame yourself.

The clinician may check for diabetes or gestational diabetes, an underactive thyroid, kidney or liver disease, and medicines that can raise triglycerides. The tests depend on your history and results. Bring a complete list of prescriptions, supplements and non-prescription products; do not stop an essential medicine without advice. Treating a contributing condition is part of lowering the risk.

What the risks mean for you and the baby

The main immediate concern with very high triglycerides is acute pancreatitis, inflammation of the pancreas that needs hospital care. A blood result cannot diagnose it by itself, and abdominal pain can have other causes in pregnancy. Do not dismiss new pain as a normal effect of pregnancy or wait to see whether a diet change helps.

Higher pregnancy lipid levels have been associated with gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and a larger baby, but these links do not predict an individual outcome or show that triglycerides alone caused it. Pre-eclampsia is a blood-pressure-related pregnancy condition; it is not another name for birth before 37 weeks. A raised triglyceride result also does not by itself diagnose a blood clot or justify starting a blood thinner.

Change food choices while protecting pregnancy nutrition

A practical starting point is to reduce sugary drinks, sweets and frequent refined-carbohydrate snacks, and choose higher-fibre bread, oats, other whole grains, vegetables, pulses and suitable portions of fruit. Include adequate protein and pregnancy-safe dairy or appropriate alternatives. Rice, bread or potatoes do not all have to disappear: portions, preparation and the overall pattern matter. Any diabetes eating plan also needs coordination with your glucose treatment.

Severe hypertriglyceridaemia can require a medically supervised low-fat or very-low-fat eating plan. This is more specific than ordinary healthy eating and must still provide enough energy, essential fatty acids and other nutrients for pregnancy. Ask for a registered dietitian with relevant experience. Avoid fasting, a crash weight-loss diet, an improvised zero-fat diet or replacing meals with supplements. The goal is appropriate pregnancy nutrition and weight gain, not rapid weight loss.

Keep activity realistic and individual

For an uncomplicated pregnancy, general guidance is to work towards about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, as you are able. Walking is one option; shorter sessions count. Someone who has been inactive can start gently rather than attempting a fixed half-hour session on five days immediately.

Ask the maternity team how any pregnancy complication or other condition changes the plan. Choose activities with a low risk of falling or being hit, stay hydrated and stop if you feel unwell. Exercise supports health and the wider treatment plan; it cannot guarantee a normal triglyceride result or replace assessment of a severe elevation.

When dietitian and specialist care matter

A severe result is a reason for coordinated maternity and lipid-specialist care, often with endocrinology or other services for an underlying condition. A registered dietitian can translate the medical plan into meals you can manage and check that restrictions do not cause nutritional gaps. You can ask for this help before reaching 500 mg/dL; it is particularly important with severe elevation or previous pancreatitis.

Agree who will review each result, when the next test is due, which symptoms need urgent help and how to make contact between appointments. If triglycerides remain high, the response is reassessment and possible treatment escalation, not an automatic referral to a blood specialist alone. A medicine-exposure registry may be offered for a particular product or research programme, but enrolment is not a universal part of treatment.

Prescription treatment is a benefit–risk decision

Current guidance allows specialist consideration of prescription omega-3 ethyl esters or a fibrate for severe fasting triglycerides of at least 500 mg/dL alongside lifestyle treatment. Fibrates are considered after the first trimester, when the expected benefit justifies the potential fetal risk. This is an individual decision based on the level and trend, previous pancreatitis, other conditions and response to treatment; reaching one number does not automatically mean starting a drug.

Pregnancy safety data are limited. Prescription omega-3 products have defined ingredients and concentrations; an over-the-counter fish-oil or routine prenatal DHA supplement is not an equivalent treatment. Capsule counts cannot be transferred between products. The prescriber chooses the formulation and dose and considers allergies, other medicines and necessary blood monitoring. Do not start, substitute, stop or increase treatment on your own; neither omega-3 nor fibrates can be described as completely risk-free in pregnancy.

If levels remain very high or pancreatitis is suspected

Persistent severe elevation may need more frequent review, a revised nutrition plan or hospital treatment. Selected patients may be offered plasma exchange, which removes and replaces part of the blood plasma, to lower triglycerides rapidly. It requires specialist judgement and appropriate facilities; it is not routine treatment for every raised result.

Suspected pancreatitis needs urgent hospital assessment and treatment of both the illness and its cause. Care may include fluids, pain relief and nutrition support, with close maternal and pregnancy monitoring. Lowering a laboratory value does not guarantee a particular pregnancy outcome.

Plan follow-up after birth

Triglycerides often fall after delivery, but a pregnancy-related rise can reveal an inherited or ongoing metabolic problem. Arrange follow-up rather than assuming that birth has removed the risk. A fasting lipid review at about six weeks postpartum is often useful, with earlier testing when the clinical situation requires it and review before a future pregnancy.

Medication and feeding decisions need a separate plan. Fenofibrate labelling advises avoiding breastfeeding during treatment and for five days after the last dose; other medicines have their own evidence and restrictions. Tell the team if you are breastfeeding or want to breastfeed so that treatment and feeding support can be coordinated. Do not interrupt essential treatment or infant feeding without an agreed alternative.

Symptoms that should not wait

Seek urgent assessment for new persistent upper-abdominal pain, especially with vomiting or very high triglycerides. Severe abdominal pain needs immediate emergency assessment; sudden severe pain spreading to the back, difficulty breathing, fainting or loss of consciousness also needs emergency help. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, or pain provoked by movement or touching the area, is another emergency warning. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance.

Contact maternity care immediately for a severe persistent headache, visual changes, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling or feeling very unwell, since these can indicate pre-eclampsia. Symptoms cannot reliably tell you the triglyceride level: keep scheduled blood tests even when you feel well, and use urgent care rather than an app or a diet trial when warning signs occur.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the pregnancy team to explain your fasting result, units, trend and next blood-test date, and whether a lipid specialist is needed.

Request a dietitian-led pregnancy nutrition plan and review diabetes, thyroid conditions and every medicine or supplement with the treating team.

Get the treatment, breastfeeding and urgent-contact plan in writing; use emergency care for warning signs rather than changing capsules yourself.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help keep test dates, the units and results reported by the laboratory, prescribed-treatment notes and questions for the maternity or lipid team together. It cannot interpret a severe result, diagnose pancreatitis, decide a pregnancy-safe dose or assess fetal wellbeing. A reassuring record does not override symptoms or the clinical plan.

When to seek help

A severe fasting triglyceride result needs prompt clinical planning, with urgent specialist review around 1,000 mg/dL or more even if you feel well. Persistent upper-abdominal pain needs urgent assessment; severe abdominal pain, sudden severe pain spreading to the back, breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness need emergency care. Severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain also needs emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Contact maternity care immediately for pre-eclampsia symptoms or other pregnancy warning signs. Do not self-prescribe fish oil, fibrates or a restrictive diet, or stop essential treatment without advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pregnancy normally raises triglycerides, so the result needs gestation-specific interpretation.
  • Fasting triglycerides at least 500 mg/dL are severe; risk rises particularly at 1,000 mg/dL or more.
  • Check inherited and secondary contributors, including diabetes, medicines and thyroid disease.
  • Dietitian-led nutrition and suitable activity are part of care; prescription treatment needs an individual specialist decision.
  • New severe abdominal pain or other emergency signs need immediate assessment, not a wait for another blood test.

Frequently asked questions

What can I eat to help lower triglycerides during pregnancy?

Reduce sugary drinks and frequent refined-carbohydrate snacks, choose higher-fibre foods and keep adequate pregnancy nutrition. Severe elevation may require a dietitian-led low-fat plan. Do not fast, remove all fat or carbohydrates, or aim for rapid weight loss on your own.

Can walking help?

Suitable regular activity supports health and the treatment plan. About 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly is a general goal for uncomplicated pregnancy, built up gently and adapted to your condition. It does not replace assessment or medication when needed.

When should I ask for a dietitian?

You can ask whenever food changes are difficult or triglycerides are raised. Expert nutrition care is particularly important with fasting levels of at least 500 mg/dL or a history of pancreatitis, alongside prompt review by the pregnancy and lipid team.

Are medicines allowed in pregnancy?

Sometimes the risk of untreated severe elevation justifies prescription treatment. Specialists may consider prescription omega-3 ethyl esters or, after the first trimester, a fibrate, using an individual benefit–risk assessment. Pregnancy data are limited; a fixed fish-oil capsule count is not safe advice for everyone.

Is 150 mg/dL the normal upper limit throughout pregnancy?

No. That is a common non-pregnant fasting reference value. Pregnancy raises triglycerides, and interpretation depends on gestation, baseline and the full clinical picture. Severe thresholds still matter even when some rise is physiological.

Does a high result mean pancreatitis or a problem with the baby?

No. It identifies a need to assess and manage risk, not a diagnosis or prediction. Pancreatitis requires clinical assessment, and observational links with pregnancy complications do not establish what will happen to one person.

Will the problem disappear after delivery?

Levels often fall, but follow-up can identify an inherited or persistent cause. Agree on repeat testing, commonly around six weeks, and review medicines and breastfeeding separately. Fenofibrate has specific breastfeeding restrictions.

When should I seek urgent help?

Get urgent assessment for persistent upper-abdominal pain, especially with vomiting. Severe abdominal pain, pain spreading to the back with sudden severe symptoms, breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness need emergency care. Severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain is also an emergency. Do not drive yourself. Contact maternity care immediately for pre-eclampsia symptoms or other pregnancy warning signs; do not wait for a diet change or another result.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
